title: Tire keeps losing air
h1: Why does my tire keep losing air?
metaDesc: One tire keeps going low? Answer a few quick questions to see if it's a nail, the valve, the rim seal or sidewall damage, how urgent it is, and what to ask the shop.
synonyms: tire goes low after a few days
tire pressure light keeps coming on
intro: A tire that needs air every few days usually has a small leak: a nail in the tread, a leaky valve, or a poor seal where the tire meets the wheel. Damage to the sidewall is the exception, and that one isn't safe to drive on. Answer a few questions to narrow down the likely cause and what to ask the tire shop.
safety: If you see a bulge, bubble, deep cut or cords showing on a tire, don't drive on it. Put on the spare or call roadside help.
Don't drive on a tire that's flat or badly low. It can overheat and fail, and it ruins the tire.
If a tire starts to shake, thump or pull hard while driving, slow down gently and pull over somewhere safe.
A small temporary spare is for short distances at reduced speed only, usually no more than 50 mph and about 50 to 70 miles. Check the label on the spare or your owner's manual.

q_state.q: What does the tire look like right now?
q_state.help: Use a tire gauge if you have one. The correct pressure is on a sticker inside the driver's door, not the number printed on the tire.

opts.a: It's flat, or so low it looks squashed
There's a bulge, bubble, cut or crack on the side of the tire
It looks normal but needs air every few days or weeks
All my tires drop, mostly when the weather turns cold

q_inspect.q: Inflate the tire, then look closely at it. What do you find?
q_inspect.help: Spray or brush soapy water over the tread, the valve stem and the edge where the tire meets the wheel. Growing bubbles show where air is escaping.

opts.a: A nail, screw or other object in the tread
Bubbles at the valve stem (where you add air)
Bubbles where the tire meets the wheel, or the wheel is corroded or was hit hard on a pothole or curb
The tire was plugged or patched before

result.title: The tire is too low to drive on
result.now: Don't drive on it. Put on the spare or call roadside assistance. If you have a portable inflator, you can try adding air where the car is parked.
if: If it holds air after inflating, it still needs inspecting the same day. A tire that was driven on while flat or very low can be damaged inside where you can't see it, so the spare is the safer choice for getting it there.
If it won't hold air or you see sidewall damage, use the spare and have the tire replaced.
If the tire shakes, thumps or loses air again quickly after inflating, don't drive on it.
result.why: A very low tire flexes too much, builds heat and can come apart. It also makes steering and braking less predictable. Even a short drive on a flat can ruin a tire that could have been repaired.

causes.name: Puncture from a nail or screw
causes.clues: An object in the tread, or a hiss when you add air.

causes.name: Leaking valve stem
causes.clues: Bubbles or a hiss at the valve.

causes.name: Sidewall or rim damage
causes.clues: A recent pothole or curb strike.

you: Look the tire over for nails, cuts and bulges.
Check the spare's pressure before you rely on it.
shop: Remove the tire and inspect it inside and out
Leak test in a water tank
Repair from the inside or replace

result.title: Sidewall damage usually means the tire needs replacing
result.now: Don't drive on this tire. Put on the spare or call roadside assistance, then have the tire replaced.
if: If the spare is a small temporary one, follow the speed and distance limits printed on it.
If the wheel is also bent or cracked, have it checked when the tire is replaced.
result.why: A bulge usually means the cords inside the tire are broken and only the rubber is holding the air. Cuts and cracks in the sidewall generally can't be safely repaired. The tire can burst without warning.

causes.name: Impact damage from a pothole or curb
causes.clues: A bulge appeared after hitting something hard.

causes.name: Cut from road debris
causes.clues: A visible slice or gouge in the side of the tire.

causes.name: Age or long-term underinflation
causes.clues: Fine cracks across the sidewall, or a tire more than several years old.

shop: Tire replacement
Wheel inspection for bends or cracks
Check the other tires for similar damage

result.title: Cold weather lowers tire pressure in all tires
result.now: Check all four tires when they're cold (before driving) and fill them to the pressure on the driver's door sticker.
if: If one tire keeps dropping faster than the others, it probably has its own leak. Go back and check it with soapy water.
If the tire pressure light stays on after filling all tires correctly, have the sensors checked.
If any tire looks squashed, or you see a bulge, cut or cords, don't drive on it. Put on the spare or call roadside help.
If you feel a shake, thump or pull while driving, slow down gently, pull over and check the tires.
result.why: Air contracts as it cools, so pressure drops when the temperature falls, by about 1 psi for every 10 degrees Fahrenheit. All the tires drop together, and it often turns on the tire pressure light on the first cold morning. A leak in one tire can hide behind this, so it's worth comparing the tires a week later.

causes.name: Normal pressure drop with colder weather
causes.clues: All tires are low by about the same amount, and the light comes on in the morning.
causes.against: If one tire is much lower than the rest, look for a leak.

causes.name: Tires not checked in a while
causes.clues: Tires lose a little air naturally over weeks and months.

you: Check all tires with a gauge before driving.
Recheck a week later and see if one tire dropped more.
shop: Tire pressure sensor check if the light stays on

result.title: A puncture in the tread is a likely source of the leak
result.now: Leave the object in place and have the tire inspected and repaired within a few days. Check and set the pressure before each drive until then.
if: If the hole is near the edge of the tread or on the sidewall, a shop will usually say it can't be repaired safely and recommend a new tire.
If the tire loses air quickly or goes flat, use the spare instead of driving on it.
If you feel a vibration or thump, or see a bulge, stop and put on the spare.
result.why: Nails and screws often seal themselves partly, so air leaks out slowly instead of all at once. The safe fix is to take the tire off the wheel and repair it from the inside with a patch and plug, so the shop can also check for hidden damage.

causes.name: Nail or screw in the tread
causes.clues: A shiny metal head in the tread, or bubbles around it.

causes.name: Small object that already fell out
causes.clues: A small hole that bubbles with soapy water.

you: Spray soapy water on the object to confirm it's leaking.
Note where it is: center tread, near the edge, or on the side.
shop: Remove the tire and inspect the inside
Patch-and-plug repair from the inside if repairable
Balance after repair

result.title: The valve stem appears to be leaking
result.now: Make sure the valve cap is on. If you have a valve core tool, snug the core gently, then test again with soapy water.
if: If it still bubbles, or the rubber stem is cracked, have the valve stem replaced soon.
If your car has tire pressure sensors in the valve, a shop should replace the seal or valve so the sensor isn't damaged.
If the tire is losing air quickly or is low by the time you next drive, put on the spare or have it fixed before driving.
result.why: The small spring valve inside the stem can loosen or get dirt in it, and rubber stems crack with age. Air can then seep out slowly even when the tire itself isn't damaged.

causes.name: Loose or dirty valve core
causes.clues: Bubbles from the center of the valve opening.

causes.name: Cracked or worn rubber valve stem
causes.clues: Cracks when you bend the stem gently, or bubbles at its base.

causes.name: Worn seal on a tire pressure sensor valve
causes.clues: A metal valve stem with bubbles where it meets the wheel.

you: Spray soapy water on the valve opening and the base of the stem.
Make sure a cap is fitted.
shop: Valve core or valve stem replacement
Tire pressure sensor seal service

result.title: Air may be leaking where the tire seals against the wheel
result.now: Check and set the pressure before each drive, and book a tire shop visit to have the tire taken off and the wheel edge cleaned and resealed.
if: If you see a crack in the wheel, or bubbles from the wheel itself, use the spare until it's inspected.
If the wheel is bent from a pothole, it may need repair or replacement. A bent wheel can also cause a vibration.
If the leak gets fast enough that the tire goes flat overnight, or you feel a new vibration or thump, use the spare.
result.why: The tire seals against a smooth lip on the wheel. Corrosion, dirt or a bend from an impact can break that seal so air seeps out slowly. It's common on older aluminum wheels and in places where roads are salted. A shop will usually test the wheel in water and check it for bends and cracks before deciding whether it can be resealed.

causes.name: Corrosion on the wheel's sealing edge
causes.clues: Older aluminum wheels, salty winters, and bubbles at several spots around the rim.

causes.name: Bent wheel from an impact
causes.clues: The leak started after a pothole or curb strike, or there's a new vibration.

causes.name: Cracked wheel
causes.clues: Bubbles from a spot on the wheel itself, not where the tire meets it.

you: Spray soapy water all the way around the edge where the tire meets the wheel.
Look at the wheel lip for dents or flat spots.
shop: Dismount, clean and reseal the tire bead
Wheel runout check for bends
Wheel crack inspection

result.title: The earlier repair may be failing
result.now: Have the tire inspected within a few days and ask the shop to check the old repair from the inside.
if: If the old repair is a plug pushed in from the outside only, ask about a proper inside repair or a new tire.
If the repair is near the edge of the tread or the tire was driven on flat, a shop will often recommend replacing it.
If the tire goes low quickly, shakes or thumps, or you see a bulge, use the spare instead of driving on it.
result.why: A plug put in from the outside, without a patch on the inside, can work loose over time. Shops also find that a tire driven while low may have hidden inner damage that makes a new repair unsafe.

causes.name: Outside-only plug working loose
causes.clues: Bubbles at the old plug.

causes.name: Second puncture nearby
causes.clues: Bubbles at a different spot in the tread.

you: Spray soapy water over the old repair.
shop: Inside inspection of the tire
Proper patch-and-plug repair or replacement

result.title: A slow leak you can't see is best found by a tire shop
result.now: Check the pressure before each drive and book a tire shop to find the leak. Note how many pounds it loses per day.
if: If it starts going low overnight or faster, get it in sooner and use the spare if needed.
If the tire pressure light flashes for a minute and then stays on, the system itself may have a fault.
If you see a bulge, cut or cords, or feel a vibration or thump, don't drive on the tire. Use the spare.
result.why: Many leaks are tiny: a small object hidden in a tread groove, a pinhole, or corrosion under the wheel edge. A shop can dunk the wheel in water to find exactly where air is escaping.

causes.name: Small puncture hidden in the tread
causes.clues: The leak is steady no matter the weather.

causes.name: Leak at the wheel edge
causes.clues: Older wheels, or a recent pothole.

causes.name: Valve stem leak
causes.clues: A missing cap or an old rubber stem.

you: Check the tire with a gauge each morning and note the readings.
Spray soapy water over the whole tire and the valve.
shop: Water tank leak test
Inside inspection of the tire
Valve and wheel edge check
